subtitle: Window switcher with previews
promotionalText: Every open window as a small live preview in one floating panel. Click to switch, drag it anywhere, or snap it onto the window you're in. Free, with no in-app purchases.
description:
Bubbleg puts every open window one click away. Each window becomes a small live preview in a floating panel, in the order you opened them, with the one you're in ringed. Your windows stay exactly where they are.

CLICK TO SWITCH
Click a bubble and its window comes to the front, even if it's minimized or in another app.

PUT IT ANYWHERE
Drag the panel by its background. It clicks into the middle of each screen edge and into each corner, and turns into a column at the sides and a row at the top or bottom.

SNAP IT TO YOUR WINDOW
Drop it next to the window you're working in and it attaches to that side. From then on it follows whichever window is active, slides along with it as you move it, and tucks inside as a thin line when there's no room outside.

MAKE IT YOURS
Preview size, spacing, corner radius, hover size, background, app icons, thumbnail sharpness and refresh rate, all adjustable. Light, dark, or follows the system. Pause it from the menu bar whenever you like.

PRIVATE BY DESIGN
Bubbleg needs Accessibility to see and switch windows, and Screen Recording to draw the previews. Previews are made on your Mac, kept in memory only, and never leave it. Bubbleg collects no data and never connects to the internet.

Free, with no in-app purchases. Requires macOS 14 Sonoma or later. Works on the main display.

review.notes:
Bubbleg is a window switcher. It shows every open window as a small live preview in a floating panel, and clicking a preview brings exactly that window to the front.

WHY ACCESSIBILITY (please also see our reply in the Resolution Center)
Bubbleg uses Accessibility for two things only:
- to list the standard windows of running apps, with their titles and positions, so each window gets a bubble;
- to bring the one window the user clicked to the front, unminimizing it first if needed.
It never reads content inside windows, never sends keystrokes or clicks to other apps, never moves, resizes or closes other apps' windows, and never acts without a click from the user. It makes no network connections and collects no data.

This is an accessibility aid: it gives every window one large, fixed, always-visible target, replacing multi-finger gestures (Mission Control), key chords (Command-Tab then Command-backtick) and hunting through overlapping windows with a single click. That helps people with limited dexterity or tremor, people using a head pointer, mouse keys or Switch Control, and people with low vision or attention differences who benefit from previews in a fixed order.

There is no alternative API: macOS offers no public way other than Accessibility to bring a specific window of another app to the front or unminimize it. NSRunningApplication can only activate an app as a whole, which shows whichever window that app used last. Bubbleg uses public API only.

Screen Recording: used only to draw each window's preview thumbnail with ScreenCaptureKit. Thumbnails stay in memory, are never saved or sent anywhere.

HOW TO TEST
1. Launch Bubbleg. A welcome window explains both permissions; click "Open Settings" on each row and turn Bubbleg on. macOS asks to reopen the app after Screen Recording.
2. Open a few windows, including two or more of the same app (e.g. two Safari windows and a Finder window). A panel of bubbles appears, one per window.
3. Click a bubble: exactly that window comes to the front, even when it is behind other windows of the same app or minimized.
4. Drag the panel by its background to move it; drop it next to the active window to attach it there.
5. The menu bar icon has Pause/Resume, Settings (appearance, Open at login, fine-tuning) and Permissions.

The app is a menu bar app (LSUIElement), so it has no Dock icon. No sign-in is needed. "Open at login" is off until the user turns it on.
